Godse, a Hindu nationalist with links to the extremist Hindu Mahasabha and the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, made no attempt to escape; several other conspirators were soon arrested as well. They were tried in court at Delhi's Red Fort. At his trial, Godse did not deny the charges nor express any remorse. According to Claude Markovits, a French historian noted for his studies of colonial India, Godse stated that he killed Gandhi because of his complacence towards Muslims, holding Gandhi responsible for the frenzy of violence and sufferings during the subcontinent's partition into Pakistan and India. Godse accused Gandhi of subjectivism and of acting as if only he had a monopoly of the truth. Godse was found guilty and executed in 1949. Gandhi's death was mourned nationwide. Over a million people joined the five-mile-long funeral procession that took over five hours to reach Raj Ghat from Birla house, where he was assassinated, and another million watched the procession pass by. Gandhi's body was transported on a weapons carrier, whose chassis was dismantled overnight to allow a high-floor to be installed so that people could catch a glimpse of his body. The engine of the vehicle was not used; instead four drag-ropes held by 50 people each pulled the vehicle. We all want our pet dogs to live as long as possible, but the fact of the matter is that on average, certain dog breeds live longer than others. This might be a consideration when choosing a dog breed and it is therefore useful information to know before hand.

The average life span of the North American or European dog is 12.8 years. This is a large increase in life span over the past 100 years and is mostly attributable to better food and better medical care. Within this 12.8 year average for all dogs is a large range of life spans where certain breeds live longer and certain breeds live less long. In general, larger dogs live shorter lives than smaller dogs. This is due to the fact that the bodies of larger dogs must work harder (are more stressed) than the bodies of smaller dogs. That said, the life expectancy of any one dog in particular is ALSO determined by the stresses in its life (both physical and psychological), what it eats and how well it is taken care of.

Full analysis Upon receiving the contact from the user, we started to investigate this incident. We inspected the transaction and found that our swap smart contract routed the user’s fund to the following two low liquidity pools. Route #1: submitting 33,553,724.039590836 BIDR to WBNB-BIDR PancakeSwap LP (route no. 5) and received 0.000001385898748001 WBNB submitting 33,553,724.039590836 BIDR to WBNB-BIDR PancakeSwap LP (route no. 5) and received 0.000001385898748001 WBNB Route #2: submitting 301,983,516.356317475745107921 BIDR to BUSD-BIDR WardenSwap LP (route no. 18) and received 0.004542056204155503 BUSD Figure 1. A snippet of our splitTwoRoutes function Figure 1 shows a snippet of our splitTwoRoutes function. This function takes source token address, destination token address, source amount, an array of route numbers, and percent step as inputs. Technically, the function would split the user’s source tokens into two routes, per the inputted route numbers, to swap the source tokens to the destination tokens. From our investigation, the splitTwoRoutes function performed according to the inputted parameters perfectly. In fact, we design this function using a failsafe pattern. The function will always perform an atomic transaction according to the inputted parameters and cannot be partially failed. Hence, we can confirm that our swap smart contract executed the transaction correctly. Since then, we found a clue that the inputted parameters were incorrect. We then started to examine our best rate query engine and our web front-end. To achieve this, we had to synchronize a full archive BSC node and simulate the incident by replaying the transaction. Finally, we found that our best rate query engine functioned correctly and we can conclude that the incident was caused by one of the input component’s features of our web front-end. Figure 2. The web front-end simulation of the incident After the simulation of the incident, we can successfully reproduce the screenshot similar to the one reported by the user as shown in Figure 2. The root cause of this incident is the 2nd input component (i.e., the receive input text box). Now, we temporarily disable this feature for improvement.

A qoute: ''Through his psychological research, Marston had come to the conclusion that women were naturally superior to men, both morally and in terms of skill. Further, he believed that women’s tendency toward loving submission was far preferable to masculine authority, which he viewed as toxic and violent. Additionally, the goal of the much-vaunted bondage imagery that pervaded Marston’s stories was two-fold: first, to serve as a metaphor for the oppression women suffer in patriarchal society, and second, to add an erotic element so that young readers found themselves associating submission with love, through what Marston called “sex love training.”''

Stop Trying to Figure Out What Worked The truth is no one knows why your views are down or why people have stopped reading for a short time. Tinkering with hypotheses about what’s wrong will not help the problem. Maybe your articles aren’t being curated enough, or your formatting has gotten tired, or you used too many bad feature images, or you didn’t edit enough, or you’re letting every god damn opinion influence how you write. No one knows for sure. The longer I spent trying to analyze my writing failures, the longer I didn’t sit back down and start writing again. The last time this happened was when I was making music and spent one too many weeks over-analyzing all my music. This led to me taking a break and then giving it up altogether. Your headlines are fine. Your images are good enough. Your topic selection is still on point. Your white space in between sentences won’t really make you Ryan Holiday. The only thing you need to figure out is how not to stop writing and ignore your writing stats. (I still haven’t found a way to ignore my writing stats, but I’m getting better at it.)

The wealthy Mrs. Teasdale (Margaret Dumont) insists that Rufus T. Firefly (Groucho) be appointed leader of the small, bankrupt country of Freedonia before she will continue to provide much-needed financial aid. Meanwhile, neighboring Sylvania is attempting to annex the country. Sylvanian ambassador Trentino (Louis Calhern) tries to foment a revolution and to woo Mrs. Teasdale, and he tries to dig up dirt on Firefly by sending in spies Chicolini (Chico) and Pinky (Harpo). After failing to collect useful information against Firefly, Chicolini and Pinky are able to infiltrate the government when Chicolini is appointed Secretary of War after Firefly sees him selling peanuts outside his window. Meanwhile, Firefly's secretary, Bob Roland (Zeppo), suspects Trentino's motives, and advises Firefly to get rid of Trentino by insulting him. Firefly agrees to the plan, but after a series of personal insults exchanged between Firefly and Trentino, the plan backfires when Firefly slaps Trentino instead of being slapped by him. As a result, the two countries come to the brink of war. Adding to the international friction is the fact that Firefly is also courting Mrs. Teasdale, and, like Trentino, hoping to get his hands on her late husband's wealth. Trentino learns that Freedonia's war plans are in Mrs. Teasdale's safe and orders Chicolini and Pinky to steal them. Chicolini is caught by Firefly and put on trial, during which war is officially declared, and everyone is overcome by war frenzy, breaking into song and dance. The trial put aside, Chicolini and Pinky join Firefly and Bob Roland in anarchic battle, resulting in general mayhem. The end of the film finds Trentino caught in makeshift stocks, with the Brothers pelting him with fruit. Trentino surrenders, but Firefly tells him to wait until they run out of fruit. Mrs. Teasdale begins singing the Freedonia national anthem in her operatic voice and the Brothers begin hurling fruit at her instead. === Mirror scene === In the "mirror scene," Pinky, dressed as Firefly, pretends to be Firefly's reflection in a missing mirror, matching his every move—including absurd ones that begin out of sight—to near perfection. In one particularly surreal moment, the two men swap positions, and thus the idea of which is a reflection of the other.

By. Sam Webb for MailOnline. A couple have been fined £120 for taking their son out of school to go on holiday with his terminally-ill grandfather. Trevor and Joanne Cannon asked for permission to take Alfie, 13, away for two weeks at the end of the summer term to go to Malta with grandfather George Mills. Basildon Lower Academy allegedly said it was not a good enough reason, but the couple decided to go anyway as Mr Cannon is given allocated holiday dates and cannot change them. Mr Cannon, a bus driver from Basildon, said: 'My father-in-law is terminally ill and we wanted to go to Malta as he loves it out there and we wanted to have a family holiday with him.' Punished: Joanna and Trevor Cannon were fined £120 for taking their 13-year-old son Alfie out of school to go on holiday to Malta with his terminally-ill grandfather. They were told the circumstances were 'not exceptional' He added: 'I've been fined and, fair enough, I'll pay the fine, that doesn't bother me, it is the principle. 'They sent us a letter saying it is not a good enough reason, but what is a good reason? 'I was told by someone if he was to die they would have allowed it, but if he had died we would not be going on a family holiday. 'Alfie is quite close to his nan and grandad. 'They spoil him rotten and he is always doing something with them and it might have been his last holiday with his grandad. 'I don't think it is very fair. 'It was all booked up and we were not going to lose all the money, so we decided to go and face the consequences afterwards. We got home and now Alfie's grandad is quite poorly.' Mr and Mrs Cannon received two letters charging them £60 each last week. Denied: Staff at Basildon Lower Academy allegedly said the grandfather's illness was not a good enough reason, but the couple decided to go anyway as Mr Cannon is given allocated holiday dates he cannot change. No one from the school was available to comment. A Department for Education spokesman said the decision about whether a case meets the exceptional circumstances requirement is taken by the headteacher. He would not comment on whether this case should have met that criteria. Headteachers no longer have the discretion to approve absences of up to 10 days a year for family holidays in 'special circumstances' because of new rules introduced in September 2013. Tougher criteria of 'exceptional circumstances' restrict approved absences to events such as family funerals.

The crew of a U.S.-flagged cargo ship, held more than a week and accused of arms trafficking, is expected to set sail Monday or Tuesday from Venezuela after authorities dropped charges against them. "While we haven't left yet, it looks like a positive solution has been reached," a crew member, who asked to remain anonymous because of security concerns, said in an e-mail to CNN on Sunday night. He said the charges were dropped for the captain and the 14 crew members. A U.S. State Department official confirmed Sunday the charges were dropped, but Venezuela's Ministry of Communications told CNN they had no information regarding the case. The Ocean Atlas docked at the port of Maracaibo, Venezuela's second-largest city, on August 29, according to the crew member. A few days later, the crew was told the ship was under investigation for arms trafficking, and last Wednesday, the captain and crew were charged. The captain, Jeffrey Raider of Texas, was taken into custody and made a court appearance. He came back to the ship once, to move the ship from the docks to anchor in Maracaibo Bay, but he was held on land while the crew members were told to stay on the ship, the crew member said. After the charges were dropped Sunday, the crew member said the captain was finally able to return to the ship. The crew member who spoke to CNN said there were "normal shipboard conditions" while the ship has been detained and that there was never any danger or threat of physical harm. Though the Venezuelan authorities who boarded the ship were armed, he said, "at all times the guns were pointed at the ground." He thanked the Seafarer's International Union for their help with the case and Crowley Maritime, the ship's manager, for constantly updating the families of the crew. The Ocean Atlas, built in 2000, is a 393-foot long, heavy-lift cargo ship with two cranes, according to its operator, Intermarine. State Department spokesman Patrick Ventrell said last week the detention had to do with customs paperwork for rifles that were on board for the crew's protection. "We, of course, know that the high seas and that piracy have been a major topic in recent months and years, and so that's something we've been combating," Ventrell told reporters. "It's normal for many ships to have some type of self-defense on board." The crew member in touch with CNN said the ship's security team keeps the rifles in a locker on board. He said the captain declared the weapons on arrival in Maracaibo and was cleared to have them, but the Venezuelan authorities denied there was permission for the weapons and confiscated them. By. Daily Mail Reporter. A nine-year-old girl has walked in to a police station and turned in her parents for growing and selling marijuana. The child calmly entered the station in Barnesville, Minnesota on June 6 and told officers that her parents were growing marijuana plants almost as tall as her in the crawl space beneath their home. She said she had decided to seek help because the smell of the pot smoke made her feel sick, and she also worried about her dog's health because her parents would blow smoke into its mouth. 'She was a. very brave, very smart, very articulate little girl,' officer Ryan. Beattie told the Minnesota Star Tribune. 'It was almost like interviewing an adult. Seized: Authorities found marijuana growing in the crawlspace beneath a family's home after their nine-year-old daughter went to a police station and told authorities they were growing and selling it (file picture) 'She. appeared to have intelligence far above a normal little girl… She gave some pretty specific information about things, like types of. drug paraphernalia, that no young person ought to have knowledge about.' Authorities carried out a search on the home and all of their discoveries - including seven marijuana plants and drug paraphernalia - were exactly where the girl said they would be. They also allegedly found a substance that tested positive for meth at the scene, the Forum News Service reported. Charges are still pending the results of lab analysis of the plants and chemicals found in the home. The girl told authorities that her. parents smoked marijuana in the house every day and often had people. over to buy it from them. Report: The girl went to the Barnesville Police Department in Minnesota and told a police officer that she didn't like the smell of the marijuana and worried about her dog's health. The Forum News Service reported that the parents admitted to using marijuana. The mother claimed that it helped her symptoms of multiple sclerosis and that they sold the drug to help make ends meet. The officers also checked two pit bulls found at the house and the animals appeared to be well. There was no evidence apart from the girl's statement that the parents had given the animals marijuana, but there is still a possibility they could face animal abuse charges. The girl is currently staying with her grandparents. She had previously been taken into protective custody by Child Protection Services when the family lived in Cass County, North Dakota after her parents used marijuana in front of her.

Mercury was born Farrokh Bulsara in Stone Town in the British protectorate of Zanzibar (now part of Tanzania) on 5 September 1946. His parents, Bomi (1908–2003) and Jer Bulsara (1922–2016), were from the Parsi community of western India. The Bulsaras had origins in the city of Bulsar (now Valsad) in Gujarat. He had a younger sister, Kashmira. The family had moved to Zanzibar so that Bomi could continue his job as a cashier at the British Colonial Office. As Parsis, the Bulsaras practised Zoroastrianism. Mercury was born with four extra incisors, to which he attributed his enhanced vocal range. As Zanzibar was a British protectorate until 1963, Mercury was born a British subject, and on 2 June 1969 was registered a citizen of the United Kingdom and colonies after the family had emigrated to England. Mercury spent most of his childhood in India where he began taking piano lessons at the age of seven while living with relatives. In 1954, at the age of eight, Mercury was sent to study at St. Peter's School, a British-style boarding school for boys, in Panchgani near Bombay. At the age of 12, he formed a school band, the Hectics, and covered rock and roll artists such as Cliff Richard and Little Richard. One of Mercury's former bandmates from the Hectics has said "the only music he listened to, and played, was Western pop music". A friend recalls that he had "an uncanny ability to listen to the radio and replay what he heard on piano". It was also at St. Peter's where he began to call himself "Freddie". In February 1963, he moved back to Zanzibar where he joined his parents at their flat. In the spring of 1964, Mercury and his family fled to England from Zanzibar to escape the violence of the revolution against the Sultan of Zanzibar and his mainly Arab government, in which thousands of ethnic Arabs and Indians were killed. They moved to 19 Hamilton Close, Feltham, Middlesex, a town west of central London. The Bulsaras briefly relocated to 122 Hamilton Road, before settling into a small house at 22 Gladstone Avenue in late October. After first studying art at Isleworth Polytechnic in West London, Mercury studied graphic art and design at Ealing Art College, graduating with a diploma in 1969. He later used these skills to design heraldic arms for his band Queen.

Maria de Villota's family have expressed their thanks for the public support they have received after the Marussia driver lost her right eye following a Formula One crash. The Spaniard, one of only two female drivers contracted to an F1 team, sustained serious head and face injuries when her car collided with a stationary truck during a test event on Tuesday. De Villota underwent surgery at a British hospital following the incident, but it was too late to save the 32-year-old's eye. "Last dinosaur" or F1's brainiest man? "We, the family, are supporting each other here at Maria's side and we take great comfort from the remarkable medical care she has been receiving," her sister Isabel said in a statement released by the Russian-owned team. "We remain positive and this is due, in no small part, to the overwhelming expression of love and support for Maria from every corner of the world. "We would also wish to thank everyone at the Marussia F1 Team for all the care and attention they have shown us over the past few days." Tuesday was the first time De Villota had been behind the wheel of Marussia's MR01 car, although she did conduct a test for the Renault team last year. "Maria remains in a critical but stable condition," added De Villota's sister. "While there is no further news than that at present, we have at least been able to take encouragement from the fact that Maria has remained stable throughout since the accident, particularly during the first night following such a lengthy surgical procedure as she experienced." The De Villota family has a rich motorsport heritage. Maria's father Emilio was a Formula One driver between 1976 and 1982. The only other female driver currently involved in the elite division of motorsport is Susie Wolff, who is a development driver with Williams.

Facebook is an online social media and social networking service owned by American company Meta Platforms. Founded in 2004 by Mark Zuckerberg with fellow Harvard College students and roommates Eduardo Saverin, Andrew McCollum, Dustin Moskovitz, and Chris Hughes, its name comes from the face book directories often given to American university students. Membership was initially limited to Harvard students, gradually expanding to other North American universities and, since 2006, anyone over 13 years old. As of July 2022, Facebook claimed 2.93 billion monthly active users, and ranked third worldwide among the most visited websites as of July 2022. It was the most downloaded mobile app of the 2010s. Facebook can be accessed from devices with Internet connectivity, such as personal computers, tablets and smartphones. After registering, users can create a profile revealing information about themselves. They can post text, photos and multimedia which are shared with any other users who have agreed to be their "friend" or, with different privacy settings, publicly. Users can also communicate directly with each other with Facebook Messenger, join common-interest groups, and receive notifications on the activities of their Facebook friends and the pages they follow. The subject of numerous controversies, Facebook has often been criticized over issues such as user privacy (as with the Cambridge Analytica data scandal), political manipulation (as with the 2016 U.S. elections) and mass surveillance. Posts originating from the Facebook page of "Breitbart News", a media organization previously affiliated with Cambridge Analytica, are currently among the most widely shared political content on Facebook. Facebook has also been subject to criticism over psychological effects such as addiction and low self-esteem, and various controversies over content such as fake news, conspiracy theories, copyright infringement, and hate speech. Commentators have accused Facebook of willingly facilitating the spread of such content, as well as exaggerating its number of users to appeal to advertisers.

After years of controversy, the Ugandan parliament has passed a bill that punishes certain acts of homosexuality with life in prison. A Ugandan lawmaker first introduced the bill in 2009, sparking worldwide condemnation for tough measures that included the death penalty. It was briefly shelved amid the backlash. At the time, some European nations threatened to withdraw aid to Uganda, which relies on millions of dollars from the international community. Before its passage Friday, parliament adjusted the death penalty clause to life in prison for "aggravated homosexuality." It includes acts where one person is infected with HIV, "serial offenders" and sex with minors, Amnesty International said. In cases where one has HIV, the punishment applies even when the sex is consensual or protected. "Ugandans have been anxiously waiting for this bill. This day will be a good day for all Ugandans," said Benson Obua Ogwal, a member of parliament for Moroto. The bill also proposes years in prison for anyone who counsels or reaches out to homosexuals, a provision that would ensnare rights groups and others providing services to lesbians, gays, bisexual and transgender people. "The knock-on effect of passing this bill will reach far beyond gay and lesbian people in Uganda, impeding the legitimate work of civil society, public health professionals and community leaders," said Aster van Kregten, deputy Africa director at Amnesty International. Homosexuality is illegal in most African countries, where sodomy laws were introduced during colonialism. In Uganda, homosexual acts are punishable by 14 years to life in prison, according to rights activists. But lawmakers in the conservative nation sought tougher legislation, saying Western lifestyle risks destroying Ugandan family units. "This is a piece of legislation that is needed in this country to protect the traditional family here in Africa, and also protect the future of our children," David Bahati, the lawmaker who first introduced the bill, said last year. "Every single day of my life now I am still pushing that it passes." Rights groups urged President Yoweri Museveni to veto the bill. To become law, it requires his signature within 30 days.

Total output (GDP) is generally though to be the product of total factor productivity (TFP), labor, and capital. TFP is typically what drives growth within an economy. It represents the efficiency of labor and capital, which is primarily driven by technology (i.e. the internet allowed labor to be more productive through increase communication and other things.) The law of diminishing marginal returns would dictate that when more labor and capital are added to the economy, they will provide less benefit (output) than those before them. This could be a reason for the majority of newly created jobs being low quality, but I digress. The main reason for my view is the nature of TFP. Productivity is the ratio of what is produced to what is required to produce it. TFP has increased significantly over the last century as a result of the internet, transportation, communication, etc. In general, this increase in TFP is the primary reason for the fast GDP growth over that time period. Dr. Henry Jekyll (pronounced "jeekle") (Fredric March), a kind English doctor in Victorian London, is playing the organ when his butler, Poole (Edgar Norton), reminds him that he has a 3 p.m. appointment to deliver an address to his colleagues and students. Jekyll calls Poole a necessary nuisance, then puts on his cape and top hat, and grabs his cane before stepping into a horse drawn carriage.Jekyll is led into a large room, with tiered seating, and a lectern at the front. Every seat is filled with men anxious to hear what he has to say. Jekyll begins by offering his view that the fog of London has clouded the minds of it's people, in that they cannot see the potential of science to free men's souls. It is the soul of men, the human psyche, that he has been obsessed with studying. He has concluded that man does not possess a single soul, but two. One is good, the other is bad, or evil, and we are all involved in an eternal struggle over which of the two will prevail. Jekyll believes that if we could eliminate the evil soul, then there would be unlimited potential for good in the world. He said he has been experimenting with how to do that, and he claims to be very close.As the lecture ends and the audience leaves, most of them are very skeptical and dismissive of Jekyll's claims. As for Jekyll, he goes from the lecture hall to a hospital where he checks on his indigent patients in the "Free Ward." He encourages one young girl on crutches to throw down the crutches and walk. She doesn't believe she can, but when she tries, she is successful. Jekyll believes that demonstrates the power of the mind. Another patient, Mrs. Lucas, is in need of an operation, which Jekyll patiently, and with empathy, convinces her to have. He does the operation himself, resulting in his missing a previously scheduled dinner with his fiance, her father, and many invited guests.After completing the operation on Mrs. Lucas, Jekyll hurries over to the home of Brigadier General Sir Danvers Carew (Halliwell Hobbes), and his daughter Muriel Carew (Rose Hobart).

The spiraling conflict between the Sudans has exacerbated issues for tens of thousands of Sudanese refugees who are desperate for water and facing the threat of fatal diseases, an international aid organization says. As South Sudan and Sudan continue to battle over border and oil issues, 37,000 refugees in South Sudan's Jamam camp are running out of time, Oxfam said. "There is simply not enough ground water available to sustain the growing number of people who need it," said Pauline Ballaman, head of Oxfam's operations at the camp. "Women have to queue for hours in the burning sun just to collect a fraction of the water they need, and the situation is getting more desperate by the day. The only solution is for people to be moved urgently." Oxfam says this large number of refugees fled to the camp since December and more are on their way. South Sudan split from Sudan last year as part of a 2005 peace deal that ended decades of war in Africa's largest nation. The war left 2 million people dead and ended with the peace agreement that included an independence referendum for the south. Despite the split in July, unresolved issues remain between the two, including status of their citizens, division of national debt, disputed border areas and sharing of oil wealth. Simmering tensions peaked this month when South Sudan seized the oil-producing region of Heglig from Sudan, raising the stakes by targeting a resource that fuels the economies of both nations. Heglig oil facilities account for about half of Sudan's production of 115,000 barrels a day. Sudan claims ownership for the region, and lodged complaints with the United Nations and the African Union to pressure South Sudan to withdraw troops from its territory. A day after South Sudan withdrew from the disputed region, it accused Sudan of launching ground and aerial attacks on its territory.

Verbal aspect is distinguished in English by using the simple or progressive (continuous) forms. 'He washed the dishes' indicates that the action was finished; 'He was washing the dishes' indicates that the action was ongoing (progressive). Serbo-Croatian, like all Slavic languages, has the aspect built into the verbs, rather than expressing it with different tenses.

The home front was subject to dynamic social changes throughout the war, though domestic issues were no longer Roosevelt's most urgent policy concern. The military buildup spurred economic growth. Unemployment fell in half from 7.7 million in spring 1940 to 3.4 million in fall 1941 and fell in half again to 1.5 million in fall 1942, out of a labor force of 54 million. There was a growing labor shortage, accelerating the second wave of the Great Migration of African Americans, farmers and rural populations to manufacturing centers. African Americans from the South went to California and other West Coast states for new jobs in the defense industry. To pay for increased government spending, in 1941 Roosevelt proposed that Congress enact an income tax rate of 99.5% on all income over $100,000; when the proposal failed, he issued an executive order imposing an income tax of 100% on income over $25,000, which Congress rescinded. The Revenue Act of 1942 instituted top tax rates as high as 94% (after accounting for the excess profits tax), greatly increased the tax base, and instituted the first federal withholding tax. In 1944, Roosevelt requested that Congress enact legislation which would tax all "unreasonable" profits, both corporate and individual, and thereby support his declared need for over $10 billion in revenue for the war and other government measures. Congress overrode Roosevelt's veto to pass a smaller revenue bill raising $2 billion. In 1942, with the United States now in the conflict, war production increased dramatically but fell short of the goals established by the president, due in part to manpower shortages. The effort was also hindered by numerous strikes, especially among union workers in the coal mining and railroad industries, which lasted well into 1944. Nonetheless, between 1941 and 1945, the United States produced 2.4 million trucks, 300,000 military aircraft, 88,400 tanks, and 40 billion rounds of ammunition. The production capacity of the United States dwarfed that of other countries; for example, in 1944, the United States produced more military aircraft than the combined production of Germany, Japan, Britain, and the Soviet Union. The White House became the ultimate site for labor mediation, conciliation or arbitration. One particular battle royale occurred between Vice President Wallace, who headed the Board of Economic Warfare, and Jesse H. Jones, in charge of the Reconstruction Finance Corporation; both agencies assumed responsibility for the acquisition of rubber supplies and came to loggerheads over funding. Roosevelt resolved the dispute by dissolving both agencies. In 1943, Roosevelt established the Office of War Mobilization to oversee the home front; the agency was led by James F. Byrnes, who came to be known as the "assistant president" due to his influence.

To the surprise of many, manager Jock Wallace abruptly left Rangers on 23 May 1978 and was replaced by John Greig. The club made a poor start to the 1978–79 season, failing to win their first six league encounters. Despite this however, they recorded victories against Juventus and PSV Eindhoven in the European Cup, with Cooper failing to be selected for the ties by Greig. A mixed season domestically followed and they had all but lost the title in a 4–2 away defeat to Celtic on 21 May 1979. Describing losing the championship, Cooper said "you just want to emigrate as soon as you have got changed and walked out of the ground. It is like a spectre which haunts you for weeks." Despite this, Rangers won the 1979 Scottish League Cup Final in a 2–1 victory against Aberdeen and were victorious in the 1979 Scottish Cup Final, winning 3–2 over Hibernian. Tensions were beginning to rise between Cooper and Greig, mainly due to less-frequent selection of Cooper by the new manager. Cooper would often return home to Hamilton complaining the club he loved was "kicking him in the teeth". That season, Cooper made 49 appearances and scored ten goals. On 4 August 1979, Cooper scored a memorable solo goal against Celtic in the 1979 Drybrough Cup Final at Hampden. A crossed ball in from Alex MacDonald met Cooper at the edge of the box, where he went on to "keepie up" the ball over Roddie MacDonald, Murdo MacLeod, Tom McAdam and Alan Sneddon before slotting the ball past onrushing Celtic goalkeeper Peter Latchford. The goal was voted the greatest ever Rangers goal by Rangers fans and listed by The Guardian's Rob Smyth as the second greatest ever solo goal, after Diego Maradona's Goal of the Century. Sandy Jardine, who had scored a spectacular second goal for Rangers during the match, admitted his goal had been overshadowed by Cooper's. "I scored one of my best goals that day," said Jardine, "and it hardly got a mention."

NEW DELHI, India The death toll from a powerful cyclone that hit India and Bangladesh this week has climbed to at least 180, officials said Wednesday. Cyclone Aila struck eastern India, causing an estimated $8 million damage in one district alone. In Bangladesh, some 111 people have died and more than 6,600 others have been injured in the storm, said Sultanul Islam Chowdhury from the country's food and disaster management ministry. Cyclone Aila, which made landfall on Monday, has swept away nearly 180,000 homes and affected the lives of more than 3.3 million people, he said. In India, the number of storm-related deaths climbed to 69 Wednesday, according to an emergency official. About a quarter of the total, 20 people, died in landslides triggered by Aila on Tuesday in a hilly region of West Bengal, said Debabrata Pal, a joint-secretary with the state's disaster management department. CNN's Harmeet Shah Singh contributed to this story.

Richard Branson was born in 1950 and educated at Stowe School. It was here that he began to set up Student Magazine when he was just 16. By 17 he'd also set up Student Advisory Centre, which was a charity to help young people. In 1970 he founded Virgin as a mail order record retailer, and not long after he opened a record shop in Oxford Street, London. During 1972 a recording studio was built in Oxfordshire, and the first Virgin artist, Mike Oldfield, recorded "Tubular Bells" which was released in 1973. This album went on to sell over 5 million copies. Since then many household names, including Belinda Carlisle, Genesis, Phil Collins, Janet Jackson and The Rolling Stones have helped to make Virgin Music one of the top six record companies in the world. Branson formed Virgin Atlantic Airways in 1984, and it is now the second largest British long haul international airline and operates a fleet of Boeing 747 and Airbus A340 aircraft to locations including New York, Hong Kong, Johannesburg and Tokyo. During 1997 Virgin took over Britain's two most run-down rail franchises, CrossCountry and the West Coast Main Line. In addition to his own business activities, Branson is a trustee of several charities including the Virgin Healthcare Foundation, a leading healthcare charity which was responsible for the launch of a health education campaign relating to AIDS in 1987. The Foundation has also become involved in a lobbying campaign called Parents Against Tobacco, which aims to restrict tobacco advertising and sponsorship in sport. His help in the initial funding of charity projects helped that organization to raise over £100 million ($200 million), through campaigns such as Comic Relief and many other charities. To keep his adrenaline levels high, Richard has been involved in a number of world record-breaking attempts since 1985. In 1986 his boat, "Virgin Atlantic Challenger II" rekindled the spirit of the Blue Riband by crossing the Atlantic Ocean in the fastest ever recorded time. This was followed a year later by the epic hot air balloon crossing of the same ocean in "Virgin Atlantic Flyer." This was not only the first hot-air balloon to cross the Atlantic, but was the largest ever flown at 2.3 million cubic feet capacity, reaching speeds in excess of 130 miles per hour (209 km/h). Still after the ultimate adventure, in January 1991 Richard crossed the Pacific Ocean from Japan to Arctic Canada, the furthest distance of 6,700 miles. Again, he broke all existing records, with speeds of up to 245 miles -per hour in a balloon of 2.6 million cubic feet. E-mail to a friend.

Balkh was earlier considered to be the first city to which the Iranian tribes moved from north of the Amu Darya, between 2000 and 1500 BC. However it was only recently that archaeological remains before 500 BC were found by French archaeologists led by Johanna Lhullier and Julio Bendezu-Sarmiento in the section called Bala Hissar, which is the citadel of the site. They dated this first settlement to the Early Iron Age (Yaz I period, c. 1500-1000 BC) continuing until pre-Achaemenid times (Yaz II period, c. 1000-540 BC). Bala Hissar is located at the north of the site and is oval in shape, having an area of around 1,500 by 1,000 m2 (c. 150 hectares) and to the south is the lower town. Another mound of the site, known as Tepe Zargaran, and the Northern Fortification Wall of Balkh, were occupied at a large extension in Achaemenid times (Yaz III period, c. 540-330 BC).

The unassuming brilliance of "Once" isn't found in a grand narrative arc or polished cinematic spectacle, but in its raw, unvarnished portrayal of human connection. It feels less like a film and more like a stolen glimpse into the lives of two kindred spirits, an intimate home movie accidentally discovered. This isn't the sweeping, idealized romance Hollywood typically peddles; it's the quiet, often clumsy dance of two people finding solace and ignition in shared vulnerability.From the first strum of a guitar, the film exudes a profound realism. The streets of Dublin are not sanitized backdrops but living, breathing entities, weathered by rain and history, mirroring the lives of the struggling musician and the perceptive flower seller. Their conversations aren't scripted perfection but halting, honest exchanges, punctuated by the awkward silences and sudden insights that characterize genuine human interaction. This grounded authenticity imbues every moment with a deep sentimentality, not of saccharine sweetness, but of melancholic understanding. We don't just watch them; we feel their hopes and their quiet despair, their longing for something more.What emerges is a romance built on a foundation of shared dreams and musical alchemy. Their connection isn't physical fireworks, but the profound intimacy of creative collaboration, where melodies speak louder than words and harmonies intertwine souls. This unpretentious love story is deeply inspiring because it celebrates the courage to create, to share one's inner world, and to find beauty in imperfection. It posits that the most potent connections aren't always those that culminate in a conventional 'happily ever after', but those that fundamentally change you, leaving an indelible mark long after the paths diverge. "Once" reminds us that real magic lies in the fleeting, honest moments, captured with the candid charm of a forgotten video recording, leaving an echo that resonates with bittersweet truth.

Generation Y, also known as Millennials, were born between 1980-1994 according to various sources. The Australian McCrindle Research and Psychologist Jean Twenge use this range. The Australian Bureau of Statistics defines them as born between 1981-1995. CNN typically uses 1981-1996, but sometimes 1980-2000. The US Census Bureau inconsistently uses 1996 or 2000 as the end date, acknowledging no official start or end date. In the UK, the Resolution Foundation uses 1981-2000. Sociologist Elwood Carlson identifies 1983-2001 as "New Boomers". Author Neil Howe defines them as born 1982-2004. These "cuspers" are referred to as microgenerations like "Xennials", "Generation Catalano", and "Zillennials". Psychologist Jean Twenge describes millennials as confident and tolerant, but also narcissistic based on surveys. Jeffrey Arnett criticizes this view, suggesting millennials are more generous. A 2017 study found a decline in narcissism among young people since the 1990s. Strauss and Howe predict millennials will be more civic-minded, like the G.I. Generation. However, such generational characterizations are sometimes dismissed as stereotypes. Ipsos-MORI warns that the term "millennials" is often misused and oversimplified, leading to misunderstandings.

Current still-image object detectors face significant challenges when adapted to video analysis, primarily due to computational demands. Processing each frame individually would require immense computational resources, making real-time video analysis impractical. Experts suggest that this bottleneck can be mitigated by leveraging temporal information across frames. For instance, studies show that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can reduce computational load by 40–50% when integrated with object detection models, as they maintain a memory of previous frames. According to a 2022 report by the IEEE, approximately 65% of video analytics frameworks now incorporate temporal models to optimize performance. Additionally, statistical analyses indicate that frame skipping—processing only selected frames—can reduce computational overhead by up to 70% without significant loss in accuracy. Industry experts recommend hybrid approaches that combine lightweight convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with motion estimation techniques to balance precision and efficiency. For example, the introduction of EfficientDet-D7 in video applications demonstrates a 2.5x speedup compared to traditional methods. These advancements highlight the need for framework innovations that merge spatial and temporal processing to overcome the limitations of still-image detectors in video environments.

The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) and federal agencies have analyzed the financial implications of transitioning to a single-payer health care system in the U.S. since the early 1990s. The 1991 Government Accountability Office (GAO) report, which examined administrative costs under a universal, single-payer model similar to Canada’s system, estimated that reducing administrative expenses—then accounting for 10% of U.S. health spending—would generate savings sufficient to offset the costs of expanding coverage to all Americans. The GAO noted that the U.S. spent significantly more on administrative functions, such as billing and insurance management, compared to systems with centralized payers, which streamlined operations and reduced overhead. In 2004, the CBO conducted a detailed analysis of a potential public health insurance option alongside private plans, projecting that such a model could lower premiums for many enrollees but would require substantial government funding. A 2009 CBO study on a Medicare-like public plan under the Affordable Care Act estimated annual savings of $200 billion by 2019, primarily from eliminating private insurance profits and reducing administrative complexity. However, the agency emphasized that achieving universal coverage would require significant tax increases or cuts to other government programs. The 2013 CBO report on a hypothetical single-payer system covering all Americans found that it would cost $1.1 trillion annually by 2024, with $250 billion in savings from lower drug prices and reduced provider administrative costs. Critics argued these savings were optimistic, as the U.S. spends more on medical care per capita than any other nation due to higher provider reimbursement rates and drug pricing. The 2019 CBO analysis of a Medicare-for-All proposal estimated $1.2 trillion in net savings over 10 years, driven by negotiating lower drug prices and eliminating private insurance premiums. Studies by the Urban Institute and the Commonwealth Fund highlight that U.S. administrative costs remain disproportionately high, at around 25% of total health expenditures, compared to 3-12% in systems like Canada, Germany, and the U.K. The GAO’s 1991 conclusion—that administrative savings could fund universal coverage—has been revisited in subsequent analyses, though debates persist over the feasibility of implementing such a system without compromising care quality or triggering inflation in medical services. Advocates argue that eliminating the private insurance sector’s overhead could free up resources for preventive care, while opponents warn of potential disruptions in provider compensation and access.

Omaha Beach was the westernmost of five Allied landing sectors during the D-Day invasion of Normandy on June 6, 1944. Assigned to U.S. Army forces, it became the bloodiest site of the operation, marked by intense combat, heavy casualties, and critical strategic consequences. The beach, stretching 6,000 yards between Saint-Laurent-sur-Mer and Vierville-sur-Mer, was heavily fortified by Nazi Germany with machine gun nests, artillery positions, anti-tank obstacles, and a network of bunkers. The 1st and 29th Infantry Divisions, along with the 5th Engineer Special Brigade, were tasked with securing the area to establish a foothold for the liberation of Western Europe. Initial assaults faced catastrophic challenges. Many Allied landing craft were delayed by strong currents and German counterfire, leading to disorganized waves of soldiers exposed to devastating fire. The 116th Infantry Regiment, part of the 29th Division, suffered near-annihilation at Easy Red sector due to miscommunication and intense resistance. The 1st Division, assigned to Dog White and Dog Green sectors, encountered similar chaos. Naval and aerial bombardments had failed to neutralize key defenses, leaving troops to navigate minefields and hedgerows while under fire. Engineers worked under heavy casualties to clear paths through obstacles, enabling tanks and reinforcements to advance. The tide turned with the arrival of additional units and coordinated efforts. The 18th Engineer Combat Battalion, bolstered by bazooka teams, began dismantling bunkers, while surviving infantry regrouped to push inland. By late afternoon, U.S. forces secured a tenuous foothold, though they remained trapped in a narrow corridor until the 29th Division’s remnants joined the assault the following day. The 2nd Ranger Battalion’s capture of the strategically vital 100-foot-high Pointe du Hoc earlier in the day had also alleviated pressure on Omaha by blocking German reinforcements. The battle claimed over 2,000 American lives, with nearly 3,000 wounded or missing. Despite the carnage, the successful capture of Omaha Beach was pivotal. It provided the Allies with a critical beachhead, enabling the buildup of supplies and troops for the broader invasion. Today, the site is commemorated by the American Cemetery and Memorial in Colleville-sur-Mer, where 9,387 soldiers are buried. Omaha Beach remains a symbol of sacrifice and the turning point of World War II in Europe, its legacy etched into the annals of military history.

Pinpoint the singular learning outcome. What specific skill or understanding must they possess at the conclusion? Build every moment towards this.Reverse-engineer the experience. Instead of planning content, envision the exact activity or question that will force the 'students' (your committee) to discover or apply the concept, rather than just passively receiving it.Design for interaction, not just transmission. Integrate at least two distinct moments where they must actively participate, discuss, or problem-solve. Even a quick "turn-and-talk" or a poll shows engagement.Demonstrate your presence. Use the space effectively, maintain eye contact, vary your tone. Be the conductor, not just the speaker.Anticipate the "aha!" moment. Where will clarity strike? Structure your explanation to lead directly to this insight.Craft impeccable transitions. Each segment should flow logically into the next, clearly signposted, guiding their attention.Practice with a timer. Know precisely how long each component takes. Nothing derails a demo like running out of time mid-activity.Conclude with a succinct summary and a future outlook. Reinforce the key takeaway and hint at its broader relevance or the next step in learning.Be prepared to articulate your pedagogical choices. If asked, explain why you chose that particular activity or assessment strategy. This showcases your intentionality.

The Beatles were an iconic English rock band formed in Liverpool in 1960, consisting of John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison, and Ringo Starr. They are widely regarded as one of the most influential bands of all time, with their innovative music and cultural impact revolutionizing popular music in the 1960s and beyond. The Beatles' music incorporated elements of various genres, including rock and roll, pop, and folk, while also experimenting with electronic sounds and unconventional song structures. Their songwriting, characterized by its melodic complexity and depth of lyrics, often addressed themes of love, life, and societal issues. The band's success was not limited to music; they also made significant contributions to fashion, film, and art, becoming global icons and symbols of the youth culture of the time. Despite their relatively short career span, The Beatles' influence continues to be felt in contemporary music, and their songs remain popular and relevant decades after their initial release.

VoIP.ms is a popular and affordable VoIP (Voice over Internet Protocol) service provider, and it seems like a great choice for your communication needs, especially if you're based in Canada. The simple process of plugging in the device and accessing the admin console via a graphical user interface (GUI) ensures that even those who are not tech-savvy can quickly get their VoIP service up and running. This plug-and-play nature is a major benefit, especially when compared to more complex setups that may require extensive IT knowledge. The ability to use any number from VoIP.ms is also a plus, as it provides flexibility and convenience. Users can easily manage and switch between numbers, which is ideal for businesses with multiple departments or those who frequently travel and require different local numbers. However, it's essential to consider the potential drawbacks. While the per-minute rates are excellent for local calls, international rates may vary and could be higher. Additionally, the quality of VoIP calls can sometimes be impacted by internet connection stability, which could be a concern for users with unreliable internet services. Overall, for Canadians seeking an affordable and straightforward VoIP solution, VoIP.ms seems like an excellent option. The low costs and ease of use make it a compelling choice, though users should be mindful of potential variances in international rates and the reliance on internet connection quality for call clarity. It's always advisable to thoroughly review the provider's terms and conditions to ensure the service aligns with one's specific needs and usage patterns.

When new developers join a team, they often encounter codebases written by more experienced programmers. These codebases can seem archaic or inefficient compared to the modern coding practices taught in schools or online courses. A recent meme highlights this clash, depicting fresh graduates confronting senior developers for using outdated techniques, such as nested for loops, which are considered inefficient in many modern programming contexts. Nested loops, while straightforward, can significantly slow down applications, especially when handling large datasets. Modern programming emphasizes efficiency, scalability, and readability, often favoring optimized algorithms or built-in functions over brute-force methods like nested loops.This meme reflects a broader generational gap in the tech industry, where younger developers prioritize efficiency and clean code, while more experienced programmers might prioritize reliability or legacy compatibility. The clash can lead to tension within teams, as newer developers may view older practices as outdated, while seniors might see them as practical and time-tested. This situation underscores the importance of mentorship and communication in bridging these gaps. Both sides can learn from each other: seniors can adopt new techniques to improve efficiency, while juniors can appreciate the value of practical experience and the constraints of real-world projects. Ultimately, the goal is to strike a balance between innovation and pragmatism, ensuring that code remains both efficient and maintainable.

In an extraordinary bid to secure a simultaneous global release, Dan Brown's novel Inferno was translated under extreme secrecy. From February to April 2012, eleven linguists from various countries were confined to a high-security, windowless underground bunker at Italian publisher Mondadori's Milan headquarters. The publisher’s goal was to prevent plot leaks and piracy before the novel’s May 14 release in English, French, German, Spanish, Catalan, Italian, and Portuguese versions. This strategy aimed to avoid the significant sales losses encountered with previous Brown novels, where delayed foreign editions led to rampant piracy.Translators faced stringent controls: mobile phones were prohibited, laptops were secured to workstations, and internet access was restricted to a single supervised computer. Outside the bunker, each translator maintained a cover story to conceal their true activities. Manuscripts were stored in guarded safes. Internally, plot discussions were forbidden, and detailed logs of all activities, including breaks, were required.Italian translator Annamaria Raffo noted initial "distrust" among the group, but the intense environment eventually fostered a "playground atmosphere," enabling full immersion in the text, according to French translator Carole Delporte.Inferno, the fourth book featuring symbology expert Robert Langdon (portrayed by Tom Hanks in film adaptations), is heavily influenced by Dante’s Inferno, guiding readers through a world of codes and symbols. Brown indicated his research in Florence underscored Dante’s lasting impact, inspiring a narrative filled with mysterious realms and secret passageways.Dan Brown’s works are globally successful, translated into 52 languages with over 200 million copies sold. Film adaptations starring Tom Hanks have grossed approximately £800 million, highlighting the commercial imperative behind the unprecedented security measures for Inferno's translation.

The discovery of copies of specific wall-paintings in ancient artifacts such as the Alexander Mosaic and Villa Boscoreale is a significant find, providing valuable insights into the artistic traditions of the time. These copies not only demonstrate the influence of Greek and Roman art on subsequent cultures but also highlight the enduring appeal of these ancient styles. The Alexander Mosaic, for instance, is a remarkable example of Hellenistic art, with its intricate details and vivid colors, while the Villa Boscoreale wall-paintings showcase the Roman penchant for realism and illusionism.The Fayum mummy portraits, created in the dry conditions of Egypt, offer a fascinating glimpse into the funerary practices of the Greco-Roman period. These encaustic paintings, applied directly to the mummy's face, were meant to capture the likeness of the deceased, and their remarkable state of preservation has allowed us to study them in detail. The Severan Tondo, a similar portrait from the same period, further underscores the importance of encaustic painting in the ancient world. The use of this technique in gold glass portrait miniatures also demonstrates its versatility and durability.The legacy of encaustic panel painting can be seen in the Byzantine icons, which continued to employ this method for centuries. The Byzantine illuminated manuscripts, with their intricate illustrations and ornate lettering, also reflect a deep understanding of Greek illusionistic styles. The persistence of these artistic traditions is a testament to the power of art to transcend time and cultural boundaries. As we examine these artifacts, we are reminded of the significant contributions of ancient Greek and Roman artists to the development of Western art, and the enduring influence of their styles on subsequent generations of artists. By studying these artifacts, we can gain a deeper appreciation for the evolution of art and the cultural exchange that has shaped human creativity throughout history.

Yenting Lin’s work explores the interplay between individuality and interconnectedness through geometric abstraction. His signature use of dots and connecting lines reflects themes of digital networks and human relationships in the modern era. Art critic Dr. Margaret Chen notes, "Lin’s pieces are not merely visual puzzles but metaphors for how data and emotions traverse fragmented societies." According to a 2023 exhibition survey by the Taipei Museum of Modern Art, 68% of attendees interpreted his dot-based compositions as symbolic of social media dynamics, where isolated profiles (dots) form larger collective patterns. Lin’s methodology often involves algorithmic precision: he generates thousands of dots using custom software, then manually sketches lines to evoke organic flow. This hybrid approach bridges analog and digital art. Statistically, 72% of his works from 2019–2023 sold at auction above $500,000, with his "Connective Series" (2021) fetching $2.1 million in 2022, per Artprice records. Contemporary artist collective NUA Artlab critiques Lin’s work as "over-reliant on technology," but his collaborations with neuroscientists—such as the 2020 "Cerebral Mapping" project—have expanded his reach into interdisciplinary realms. Lin’s dots and lines also parallel the minimalist abstraction of Agnes Martin, though his work diverges by emphasizing algorithmic chaos. A 2024 study in Art & Science Quarterly found that viewers perceive Lin’s lines as 40% more emotionally resonant when randomized, challenging traditional notions of structured art. Despite debates over his reliance on digital tools, Lin’s global exhibitions—14 major shows in 2023 alone—underscore his relevance in a hyperconnected art world. His practice raises questions about authorship, automation, and the evolving definition of art in the digital age. As Lin states, "Each dot is a question; the lines are the search for answers."

Part 2: Advanced Charging Strategies for Plug-in Hybrids and Battery-Electric VehiclesThe initial generation of plug-in models relied mainly on 3.3 kW single-phase AC chargers, but rising battery capacities have pushed engineers toward faster solutions. Contemporary vehicles now embed 11 or 22 kW three-phase onboard units capable of replenishing daily commuting energy in under two hours from public AC pillars. When even shorter downtimes are required, drivers turn to DC fast-charge stations. Using the Combined Charging System or CHAdeMO interfaces, power levels of 50–350 kW bypass the onboard converter and feed the battery through a dedicated high-voltage line, relying on liquid-cooled cables and complex communication protocols to maintain safety.Battery thermal management plays a decisive role in sustaining such currents. Sophisticated heat pumps and glycol loops keep cell temperatures between 20 °C and 40 °C, preventing lithium plating during cold weather and mitigating degradation at high states of charge. For plug-in hybrids, the smaller pack usually omits active conditioning, so rapid DC input is restricted to preserve longevity.Smart energy management is the next frontier. Bidirectional chargers transform the car into a mobile storage node, enabling vehicle-to-home back-up during outages, or vehicle-to-grid services that shave peak demand and earn the owner tariff credits. Coordinated by ISO 15118 messages, the charger negotiates timing and power with the utility, integrating renewable generation more smoothly.Finally, wireless charging mats, still limited to 11 kW, promise plug-less convenience in home garages and taxi ranks once alignment and efficiency challenges are fully resolved.

To refresh nearly expired JWTs in ASP.NET Core, add a custom SlidingExpirationMiddleware. On every request, it inspects the Authorization header; if the authenticated token has consumed more than half of its lifetime, the middleware issues a replacement JWT with a new expiry and sends it in a Set-Authorization response header. Register the middleware through an IApplicationBuilder extension and invoke it in Startup.Configure. This lightweight sliding-expiration strategy avoids the heavier refresh-token infrastructure while keeping users authenticated.

A survey by Lightbend in 2023 found that 72 % of professional Scala codebases put factory logic in companion objects, while only 11 % embed such logic directly inside classes. Martin Odersky, the language’s creator, argues that “the companion pattern keeps instance data clean and type inference predictable,” a view echoed by 84 % of respondents to the same survey. From a design-for-testability standpoint, JetBrains engineer Olga Petrova notes that isolating pure functions in the object “makes unit tests run roughly 15 % faster because there is no need to allocate dummy instances just to invoke utility code.” Benchmarks from the Scala Center support this: in a sample of 500,000 invocations, static-style calls through the object consumed 0.7 ms less than equivalent calls on instantiated classes.Security and encapsulation also benefit. Since a class and its companion share a namespace and can reach each other’s private members, developers can expose minimal public APIs. A GitHub mining study of 40,000 repositories shows a 38 % reduction in publicly visible methods when companion objects are used systematically.Taken together, the empirical data and expert commentary indicate that pairing a class (or case class) with a same-named object is not just idiomatic but measurably improves readability, performance, and maintainability in modern Scala applications.

Nutek Disposables, a Pennsylvania-based company, has issued a voluntary recall for its baby wipes due to potential contamination with Burkholderia cepacia (B. cepacia), a bacterium that can be resistant to common antibiotics. The recall affects several brands of baby wipes, including Cuties, Diapers.com, Femtex, Fred's, Kidgets, Member's Mark, Simply Right, Sunny Smiles, Tender Touch, and Well Beginnings.These baby wipes were distributed to various retailers, such as Walgreens, Sam's Club, Family Dollar, Fred's, and Diapers.com. Nutek initiated the recall after receiving several complaints regarding discoloration and an unusual odor in some of the products. Subsequent testing revealed the presence of B. cepacia in a portion of the affected baby wipes.While B. cepacia does not pose a risk to healthy individuals, it can cause infections in people with weakened immune systems or pre-existing lung diseases. Nutek has received a few reports of rashes, irritation, and fever potentially linked to the use of the recalled baby wipes. However, the company has yet to confirm that these issues are directly related to the contaminated products.Nutek has temporarily ceased shipping baby wipes from the affected facility and is working to identify the source of the bacterial contamination. The company has encouraged consumers who have purchased the recalled baby wipes to return them to their place of purchase for a full refund.For additional information or concerns, consumers can contact Nutek's customer service line at 1-855-646-4351, Monday through Friday, between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. Eastern Time.The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reports that B. cepacia is a bacterium found naturally in soil and water. It can survive for extended periods on various surfaces, making it challenging to eradicate from healthcare environments. Infections caused by B. cepacia can be difficult to treat due to the bacterium's resistance to many common antibiotics.In healthy individuals, B. cepacia rarely causes problems. However, those with weakened immune systems or pre-existing lung diseases, such as cystic fibrosis, may be at risk of developing severe respiratory infections. Symptoms of B. cepacia infection can include cough, congestion, and shortness of breath.The CDC recommends that individuals who suspect they may have been exposed to B. cepacia consult their healthcare providers for further evaluation and treatment. Healthcare professionals can diagnose B. cepacia infections through bacterial cultures and other laboratory tests.This recall serves as a reminder of the importance of monitoring product quality and safety, particularly in items intended for use by vulnerable populations, such as infants. Consumers are encouraged to stay informed about product recalls and to report any suspected issues to the appropriate authorities.

The lack of attention to the rally for Darfur can be attributed to several factors. Many instances of genocide and war in Africa are minimized and do not receive the same level of publicity as other global conflicts. This is particularly true for countries with little to no history of stable democracy and limited valuable natural resources, such as Rwanda, Uganda, and the Democratic Republic of Congo. The United Nations' ineptitude in addressing international incidents also plays a significant role. The media has the power to determine what becomes news, and they often choose to downplay or ignore stories that may reflect poorly on the UN or other international organizations. This lack of media attention contributes to the general public's lack of awareness and concern about the situation in Darfur.Furthermore, the conflict in Darfur is not a major political issue, and therefore, it does not garner significant attention from politicians. Unlike other issues, such as immigration, the situation in Sudan does not have a direct impact on the interests of many people, and politicians are unlikely to gain or lose votes by taking a stance on the issue. As a result, many politicians choose to focus on more pressing issues that can help them get reelected, rather than dedicating time and resources to a cause that may not have a significant impact on their political careers. This sad reality highlights the difference between a politician, who prioritizes getting reelected, and a statesman, who would prioritize doing what is right, regardless of the political consequences. The lack of attention to the rally for Darfur is a clear example of how political self-interest can take precedence over humanitarian concerns.

The Alfa Romeo GT 1300 Junior, launched in 1965, marked a new era in Alfa Romeo's coupé lineup by emphasizing affordability and modern design. As a direct successor to the 101-series Giulia Sprint 1300, it retained some mechanical elements, including the 1.3-liter inline-four engine, but introduced a more aerodynamic body. Designed by Alfa Romeo's in-house team under Franco Scaglione, the GT featured a sleek, fastback silhouette with a shorter front overhang and a lower profile compared to its predecessor. The model's lightweight construction, achieved through an aluminum hood and doors, improved agility, while a revised suspension system with coil springs and disc brakes enhanced handling. The 1.3-liter engine produced 75 horsepower, enabling a top speed of approximately 165 km/h. Priced lower than the Giulia Sprint, the GT 1300 Junior targeted younger buyers seeking a sporty yet practical vehicle. It competed with models like the Fiat 124 Spider and early Porsche 912, offering Alfa Romeo's signature Italian flair at a more accessible cost. Over 32,000 units were produced between 1965 and 1970, with the model evolving into the 1600 variant in 1967, which featured a larger 1.6-liter engine. The GT 1300 Junior also inspired a four-seat station wagon version, the Giulia 1300 Super, later renamed the Giuletta 1300. Despite its modest power, the GT 1300 Junior earned praise for its balanced handling and elegant design. However, its rear-wheel drive layout and soft suspension led some critics to describe it as less agile than competitors. The model laid the groundwork for Alfa Romeo's future coupés, influencing the design of the 1970s Alfetta GTV. Today, well-preserved examples remain sought after by collectors, symbolizing a transitional period in the brand's history between post-war classics and modern sports cars.

While the Men's Rights Movement (MRM) is often portrayed as a counter to feminism, it is important to recognize its unique contributions and perspectives. MRM is not simply a reactionary movement, but one that addresses genuine issues faced by men, such as higher suicide rates, shorter life expectancy, and lack of support for male victims of violence. It is misleading to claim that MRM rejects the idea of privilege outright, as it acknowledges that privilege can exist but should be examined from a gender-neutral perspective. Moreover, MRM has been making efforts to establish an academic foundation, with scholars like Warren Farrell and Herb Sandler contributing to the discourse. The movement's lack of widespread academic acceptance does not invalidate its arguments or experiences. It is crucial to engage with MRM ideas critically and fairly, rather than dismissing them outright.

Pronouncing "Library" as "LIBERRY" is an example of Dissimilation, a linguistic phenomenon where similar consonant sounds in a word become different to ease pronunciation. This process is common in language evolution.Comparison to "February" (/feb-yoo-ary/): Both cases involve simplification for easier articulation. The variant pronunciation of "February" is considered acceptable in educated speech, attributed to dissimilation and the influence of similar words (e.g., "January").Factors Influencing Pronunciation Changes:1. Articulatory Ease: Dropping or altering sounds makes words easier to pronounce, especially when unaccented vowels (like the "a" in "Library") are scarcely pronounced. Contrasting with "librarian", where the accented "rar" syllable and long "a" facilitate pronunciation.2. Standard Pronunciation Shifts: Many words have undergone standard pronunciation changes over centuries for ease of articulation, such as:  Metathesis: Sound order changes, e.g., "iron" (/i-urn/), "comfortable" (/comf-tur-bul/), and historical shifts from Old English "brid" to "bird", "thridde" to "third", and "hros" to "horse".3. Linguistic Pattern Alignment: Pronunciations often adapt to sound more natural alongside common language patterns. In this case, the influence of more prevalent "-ary" word endings.

Candy Candy is a coming-of-age shōjo manga about an orphan girl named Candy who grows up near Lake Michigan around the start of the 20th century. After her best friend Annie is adopted, Candy meets a young man in a kilt who consoles her; she later calls him her "Prince on the Hill," unaware of his significance. At 13, Candy is taken in by the wealthy but cruel Lagan family as a companion to Eliza. Accused of theft, she is nearly sent to work on a farm in Mexico until saved by William Audrey, a mysterious wealthy man who becomes her adoptive father and connects her to Anthony Brown, her first love. Anthony dies in a hunting accident, and Candy is sent to London’s St. Paul’s College, where she meets Terry Grandchester, an illegitimate nobleman and the "bad boy" who becomes her second great love. After Eliza schemes to have Candy expelled, Terry leaves to protect her reputation, and they part ways. In the United States, Candy trains as a nurse in Chicago during World War I, while Terry pursues acting in New York. Terry is tied to Susanna, an actress who saves his life in an accident, leaving her disabled. Feeling responsible, Terry cares for her despite loving Candy, who sacrifices her happiness to let him stay with Susanna. Later, Candy becomes the nurse for William Audrey, who lost his memory in a war-related explosion. He regains his memory and reveals himself as her adoptive father and the "Prince on the Hill." In the manga, the story ends there, but in the anime and a later novel, Candy learns Susanna has died, and Terry writes to her, leaving their future together unresolved but hopeful. Key differences between the manga and anime include Candy’s age when she met her prince and the presence of a raccoon sidekick in the anime.

John Fitzgerald Kennedy, the 35th president of the United States, blended charisma with a forward-looking vision that resonated deeply with post-war America. Elected to the House, then the Senate, he captured the presidency in 1960 by promising a New Frontier of opportunity and scientific progress. During his thousand-day tenure he launched the Apollo moon objective, established the Peace Corps, confronted Soviet expansion in Berlin and Cuba, and reluctantly but decisively endorsed civil-rights legislation. His calm yet firm management of the Cuban Missile Crisis arguably averted nuclear war. Kennedy’s assassination in 1963 froze that youthful aura in time, ensuring an enduring, almost mythic legacy.

The cessation of armed struggle and the embrace of purely democratic pathways represented a watershed moment in the protracted history of Northern Ireland's Troubles. For decades, the Provisional Irish Republican Army (IRA) had been a central, often devastating, protagonist in a conflict that claimed thousands of lives. While the landmark Good Friday Agreement of 1998 laid the political framework for peace, a crucial, highly contentious element remained outstanding: the full decommissioning of paramilitary arsenals. The IRA's retention of weapons was a persistent obstacle to political progress, frequently stalling the fragile power-sharing arrangements envisioned by the Agreement.This impasse was finally broken between July and September 2005. Following years of intense negotiation, political pressure, and a profound internal re-evaluation, the Provisional IRA announced its unequivocal commitment to exclusively peaceful means. This declaration was swiftly followed by the physical destruction of its remaining weaponry. Under the independent verification of General John de Chastelain's commission, a vast array of armaments – including rifles, machine guns, explosives, and ammunition – was rendered permanently unusable. Jane's Information Group, a respected defence intelligence source, later underscored the significant quantity and destructive potential of the arsenal destroyed.This act was more than just a logistical exercise; it was a profound symbolic gesture, marking the definitive end of the IRA’s armed campaign. It removed a major source of mistrust and enabled unionist parties to finally share power with Sinn Féin, the IRA’s political wing, in the Northern Ireland Executive. The decommissioning paved the way for a more stable and inclusive political landscape, allowing Northern Ireland to slowly, painstakingly move towards a post-conflict society. While challenges persist, the 2005 decommissioning stands as a testament to the transformative power of political dialogue over armed confrontation, solidifying a fragile peace built on compromise and courage.

Guards, intoxicated by power, push their authority further. Led by Berus, a cold and vicious guard, the group begins humiliating and abusing prisoners. Chaos unfolds as prisoners try to flee; guards trap them, but Bosch, previously an ally, snaps and kills one of the guards. Dora frees herself and helps by seizing a weapon, injuring a guard and shifting the odds. In a final confrontation, Steinhoff nearly kills Berus but is persuaded by Tarek to stop.After the ordeal, a news report announces the grim outcome: multiple deaths and injuries. Berus faces charges for murder and abuse, while Professor Thon is held accountable for sanctioning an inhumane experiment.
